meta.name: Adesanya AI Advisory
meta.tagline: AI Law & Governance — a curated library of primary sources
meta.note: Public knowledge base. Every entry links to an authoritative, publicly accessible source (regulators, standards bodies, official texts, court records). Edit this file to add/update resources. Private/personal documents are kept OUT of this file and out of the deployed site.

documents.t: EU AI Act — full official text (Reg. 2024/1689)
documents.note: The authoritative consolidated text of the EU AI Act on EUR-Lex — all language versions and formats. The starting point for any AI Act question.

documents.t: European Commission — AI Act regulatory framework
documents.note: The Commission's official hub: risk-based approach, the phased application timeline, and links to implementing guidance and the AI Office.

documents.t: European AI Office
documents.note: The Commission body responsible for GPAI model oversight and enforcement of the EU AI Act. As of 2026 the AI Office is issuing binding decisions and formal guidance — not merely implementing structure. Key source for enforcement notices, the GPAI Code of Practice status, and prohibited practices guidance.

documents.t: General-Purpose AI Code of Practice — final text (2025)
documents.note: The final GPAI Code of Practice covering Transparency, Copyright, Safety & Security — the primary compliance route for providers of general-purpose AI models under Article 53 EU AI Act. Note: the Digital Omnibus provisional deferral (pending Council adoption as at June 2026) does not affect GPAI model obligations, which remain tied to the August 2026 horizon.

documents.t: AI Act Explorer (artificialintelligenceact.eu)
documents.note: A free, well-structured browser of the Act's articles, annexes and recitals — the fastest way to navigate to a specific provision without EUR-Lex.

documents.t: EU AI Act implementation timeline — official roadmap
documents.note: The definitive date-by-date application roadmap for the AI Act. Key horizons: prohibited practices in force from February 2025; transparency (Art.50), AI literacy (Art.4) and GPAI enforcement from 2 August 2026; full high-risk Annex III obligations provisionally deferred to 2 December 2027 (Digital Omnibus — not yet law as at June 2026).

documents.t: AI Office — Prohibited AI Practices guidance (Article 5)
documents.note: The AI Office's guidance on the six categories of AI practices banned outright under Article 5 — in force since 2 February 2025. Covers subliminal manipulation, social scoring, real-time remote biometric identification, exploitation of vulnerabilities, and AI-based emotion inference in workplace/education. Essential reading before any AI system goes to market in the EU.

documents.t: Digital Omnibus — AI Act amendment (formally adopted 29 June 2026)
documents.note: The Digital Omnibus amendment was formally adopted by the EU Council on 29 June 2026 (Official Journal publication pending as at that date). This is now law. It defers full Annex III high-risk AI obligations (Articles 9–17, Article 26 deployer requirements) from August 2026 to 2 December 2027, and Annex I product-regulated AI to August 2028. Adds new prohibition on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM (effective December 2026). Does NOT defer Article 50 transparency, Article 4 AI literacy, or GPAI obligations — those remain 2 August 2026.

documents.t: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
documents.note: The de-facto US standard for trustworthy AI — Govern, Map, Measure, Manage. Widely referenced in contracts and as evidence of reasonable care. Aligns well with ISO 42001.

documents.t: NIST Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1)
documents.note: NIST's companion profile applying the AI RMF specifically to generative-AI risks — a practical risk checklist for GenAI deployments covering 12 risk categories including hallucinations, CBRN uplift, and data privacy.

documents.t: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI Management System
documents.note: The first certifiable AI management-system standard — plan-do-check-act for AI governance. The backbone for an auditable programme. Referenced in procurement criteria by several EU member states. (Standard is paid; the ISO catalogue page is public.)

documents.t: OECD AI Principles (rev. 2024)
documents.note: The most widely adopted intergovernmental principles for trustworthy AI — the reference point underpinning many national frameworks and the basis for the EU AI Act's values architecture.

documents.t: Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI
documents.note: The first legally binding international treaty on AI — aligning the AI lifecycle with human rights, democracy and the rule of law. Signed 5 September 2024; the EU ratified on 15 May 2026. The Convention enters into force three months after five signatories (including three Council of Europe member states) have ratified. Signatories include the EU, UK, US, Canada, Japan, and numerous Council of Europe member states. Highly relevant for governance frameworks in any AI compliance programme.

documents.t: ENISA — AI Cybersecurity Threat Landscape
documents.note: ENISA's dedicated AI and cybersecurity hub — threat landscape reports, guidelines for securing AI systems, and analysis of adversarial attacks, data poisoning, and model inversion. Essential for CISO-facing AI governance work and relevant to Article 9 EU AI Act security requirements.

documents.t: EU Model Contractual Clauses for AI (MCC-AI, 2025)
documents.note: The Commission's updated model contractual clauses for AI procurement — full (high-risk) and light (non-high-risk) versions plus commentary, aligned to the AI Act. The most authoritative starting point for drafting AI procurement terms.

documents.t: SCL — AI contractual clauses & resources
documents.note: The Society for Computers & Law publishes practitioner-drafted AI contract clauses and commentary — a useful private-sector counterpart to the EU MCC-AI. Particularly strong on liability and IP allocation clauses.

documents.t: EU Data Act (Regulation 2023/2854)
documents.note: In force from 12 September 2025. The EU Data Act governs who can access and use data generated by connected devices and related services — directly affecting AI systems that process IoT or sensor data. Key implications: mandatory data-sharing obligations, switching rights, and limits on data-use exclusivity clauses in B2B contracts. Every AI contract involving device data should be reviewed against this.

documents.t: EU AI Liability Directive — withdrawn (Commission proposal, 2022)
documents.note: WITHDRAWN by the European Commission in February 2025. The specific fault-based rebuttable-presumption mechanism this directive would have created no longer exists. Civil AI liability in the EU is now governed by the revised Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853 — see 'eu-pld-2024'. This entry is retained as a historical reference only.

documents.t: EU Product Liability Directive (revised) — Directive (EU) 2024/2853
documents.note: In force 9 December 2024; member states must transpose by 9 December 2026. Explicitly classifies software and AI systems as 'products' subject to no-fault strict liability — the operative EU instrument for AI civil liability following the withdrawal of the AI Liability Directive. Applies to AI systems placed on the EU market or put into service after 9 December 2026. Key implication for contracts: liability allocation clauses and indemnities in AI procurement must be reviewed against this directive's strict-liability baseline. Covers both embedded and stand-alone software, AI-as-a-service, and digital manufacturing files.

documents.t: EDPB Opinion 28/2024 — AI models & GDPR
documents.note: The key EU privacy text on AI: when an AI model is considered 'anonymous', using legitimate interest as a legal basis for AI training, and consequences of unlawful training data. Essential reading alongside any AI procurement or development engagement.

documents.t: EDPB Guidelines 04/2019 — Automated Decision-Making (Article 22 GDPR)
documents.note: The EDPB's definitive guidance on automated individual decision-making and profiling under GDPR Article 22 — including when human review is required, what constitutes 'solely automated' processing, and the right to explanation. Directly relevant to any AI system making consequential decisions about individuals (HR, credit, insurance, access to services).

documents.t: Irish DPC — AI, LLMs & Data Protection
documents.note: The Irish Data Protection Commission's guidance on AI and large language models — directly relevant for organisations operating under Irish/EU data-protection law. The DPC is the lead EU supervisory authority for most major tech companies (Meta, Google, Apple, Microsoft, OpenAI EU operations).

documents.t: ICO — Guidance on AI and Data Protection
documents.note: The UK regulator's detailed, practical guidance on building data protection into AI systems — including the AI & data-protection risk toolkit. Particularly strong on fairness, transparency, and purpose limitation. Useful even for EU practitioners as a more detailed complement to EDPB guidance.

documents.t: CNIL — Artificial Intelligence resources
documents.note: France's data-protection authority — practical 'how-to' sheets on developing AI systems in GDPR compliance. Often ahead of other DPAs in practical guidance. Particularly useful on data minimisation, purpose limitation, and training-data compliance.

documents.t: Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA) — primary text
documents.note: The NDPA 2023 — Nigeria's GDPR-equivalent statute. Directly relevant following the June 2026 Onimisi v. GTCO Federal High Court judgment enforcing data subject rights (right to object, transparency, lawful basis) under its provisions. See 'Case Law & Enforcement' for the Onimisi case note. The NDPA mirrors GDPR Articles 5, 6, 13, 14, 17, and 21 with near-identical drafting.

documents.t: Onimisi v. Guaranty Trust Holding Company Plc (FHC/ABJ/CS/1181/2025)
documents.note: Federal High Court of Nigeria, 11 June 2026. Court declares unlawful the processing of a non-customer's personal data for direct marketing without consent, ignoring a written objection. Orders disclosure of data broker sources. Damages awarded. Key parallels: GDPR Art.6 lawful basis, Art.21 right to object, Art.13/14 transparency obligations. See the Adesanya AI Advisory case note for a full EU/GDPR implications analysis.

documents.t: Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence — district court ruling (2025)
documents.note: US District Court (D. Del.), February 2025. The first major judicial ruling on whether training an AI system on copyrighted content constitutes copyright infringement — court found against Ross Intelligence, rejecting a fair-use defence for AI training on Westlaw headnotes. Case on appeal to the Third Circuit as of 2026. Sets a significant precedent for the use of copyrighted materials in AI training datasets globally, including for EU-based operators relying on any US-generated training data.

documents.t: Clearview AI — ICO Enforcement Notice & Fine (UK)
documents.note: The ICO's enforcement action against Clearview AI — £7.5M fine and order to stop collecting UK residents' facial images and delete existing data. Part of a coordinated EU-wide enforcement wave (France CNIL, Italy Garante, Greece, Sweden also issued fines/orders). The flagship case demonstrating that web-scraping personal data to train AI systems violates GDPR/UK GDPR lawful-basis and special-category data rules.

documents.t: EDPB — Coordinated enforcement on ChatGPT/OpenAI (2024)
documents.note: The EDPB's report on coordinated DPA enforcement activity targeting ChatGPT/OpenAI across multiple EU member states. The Irish DPC is the lead supervisory authority given OpenAI's EU establishment in Ireland. Issues include: lawful basis for training data, accuracy obligations, transparency to data subjects, and age verification. The most significant ongoing GDPR-AI enforcement action in the EU — outcome will set binding precedent for all large-scale AI system operators.

documents.t: GDPR Enforcement Tracker — live database of fines
documents.note: The go-to live database of all GDPR enforcement actions, fines and decisions across EU/EEA supervisory authorities — maintained by CMS and updated continuously. Filterable by country, article, sector, and company. As of mid-2026: 2,000+ decisions logged, total fines exceeding €4.5 billion. Essential for benchmarking risk exposure and evidencing the cost of non-compliance to boards.

documents.t: TikTok v DPC — Irish High Court (3 Jun 2026)
documents.note: Irish High Court, 3 June 2026. Court upheld the DPC's €530M GDPR fine on TikTok's transfers of EEA user data to China but ordered the DPC to reconsider the corrective order suspending future transfers. DPC confirmed 12 June it will not appeal. Live precedent: Chapter V transfer restrictions apply to AI data pipelines; the Standard Contractual Clauses plus supplementary measures framework cannot bridge a conflict with Chinese intelligence law. The DPC's substantive transfer analysis now has High Court backing — directly relevant to any Irish/EU business relying on SCCs for AI data flows to third countries.

documents.t: Court of Rome — OpenAI / Garante one-stop-shop annulment (Mar 2026)
documents.note: Court of Rome, 18 March 2026. Italy's €15M GDPR fine against OpenAI annulled: once OpenAI's Irish establishment was recognised (February 2024), the Garante lost competence under the one-stop-shop mechanism and the DPC became lead supervisory authority. The substantive violations — no legal basis for training data, transparency failures, failure to notify a data breach, lack of age verification — were never examined. Critical implication: Ireland is now the de-facto lead GDPR enforcer for AI companies established in Dublin. The DPC inherits the substantive enforcement gap. A significant development for any AI company with EU operations structured through Ireland.

documents.t: CJEU — NTH Haustechnik (C-484/24), 18 Jun 2026
documents.note: CJEU, 18 June 2026. Courts that process documents containing personal data (retrieving, storing, using as evidence) are themselves subject to GDPR. Crucially, evidence obtained in breach of GDPR is not automatically inadmissible — courts must balance data-protection obligations against the right to a fair hearing and procedural rights. The two questions (was the data collected unlawfully, and may the court use it) are distinct. Relevant to: AI audit logs and logging obligations under Article 12/19 EU AI Act; AI-generated evidence in commercial disputes; discovery of AI system records in litigation.

documents.t: CJEU — Dun & Bradstreet Austria (C-203/22), 27 Feb 2025
documents.note: CJEU, 27 February 2025. Under Article 22, data controllers must provide a genuine, intelligible explanation of the logic of automated decisions — handing over the algorithm or a complex mathematical formula does not suffice. Where the controller claims trade-secret protection for its AI model, the supervisory authority or court adjudicates the balance: the controller must disclose the protected information to the authority/court, which then determines the extent of the data subject's right. Directly relevant to any AI system making or materially influencing decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. See also the SCHUFA ruling (C-634/21): if a human formally signs off but defers entirely to the algorithm in practice, the decision is still 'solely automated' under Article 22.

documents.t: Ireland National AI Strategy — 'AI: Here for Good'
documents.note: Ireland's official national AI strategy — published by the Department of Enterprise, Trade and Employment. Sets out Ireland's ambition as an AI-enabled economy. Relevant context for Irish enterprise clients and for understanding the regulatory environment Adesanya AI Advisory operates in. Note: strategy predates the EU AI Act; watch for an updated strategy aligning with the Act's requirements.

documents.t: Data Protection Commission (Ireland) — guidance & enforcement hub
documents.note: The Irish DPC is the lead supervisory authority under GDPR for most of the world's largest tech companies (Meta, Google, Apple, Microsoft, TikTok, LinkedIn, OpenAI EU). All DPC guidance, statutory codes, enforcement decisions and ongoing inquiries are published here. For any Irish-based compliance practice, this is the primary regulatory reference point — read it before advising any company with EU data flows through Ireland.

documents.t: Law Society of Ireland — AI in Legal Practice guidance
documents.note: The Law Society of Ireland's guidance on using AI in legal practice — covering professional obligations, client confidentiality, competence, and oversight requirements when deploying AI tools. Relevant for in-house counsel and legal teams in Ireland governed by Irish professional standards.

documents.t: IDA Ireland — AI capability & investment framework
documents.note: IDA Ireland's AI framework and investment positioning — useful context when advising multinational clients on Ireland as an EU AI Act compliance base. Ireland's position as lead DPA jurisdiction for most major AI operators makes its regulatory environment directly material to group-wide AI governance decisions.

documents.t: Stanford HAI — AI Index Report 2026
documents.note: The definitive annual data report on the state of AI — investment, adoption, capability and responsible-AI trends. 2026 edition: 88% organisational AI adoption; US private AI investment $285.9bn; governance frameworks still lagging capability globally. Excellent source for board presentations and thought leadership.

documents.t: OECD.AI Policy Observatory
documents.note: A live tracker of national AI policies and strategies worldwide — useful for cross-border and comparative AI-governance work. Covers 70+ countries.

documents.t: UNESCO — Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021)
documents.note: The first global standard-setting instrument on AI ethics, adopted by 193 member states in 2021. Note: this predates both the EU AI Act and the OECD 2024 revision, and does not address the EU regulatory framework. Its value is as a global values baseline and reference point for organisations operating across non-EU jurisdictions, particularly in the Global South where GDPR-equivalent law is developing.

documents.t: IAPP — AI Governance Center
documents.note: Resources, news, and the AIGP (AI Governance Professional) certification from the leading privacy/AI-governance professional body. The AIGP is becoming a market-standard credential for AI compliance professionals. Strong for ongoing CPD, practitioner guidance, and staying current with enforcement developments.

documents.t: Future of Privacy Forum
documents.note: A respected think tank publishing accessible analysis, visual explainers and policy briefs on AI, privacy and emerging-technology law. Particularly strong on US/EU comparative analysis and practical implications of new regulations for business. Useful for quick briefing materials and client-facing summaries.
